items.title: Shapes of alkanes and cycloalkanes (printed as a second 11.2.3)

source_refs.note: Shapes of Alkanes and Cycloalkanes, printed as a second 11.2.3 with Figure 11.4 and Tables 11.4 and 11.5, pages 249-251. Table 11.5 prints cyclopentane as C4H10; noted.

blocks.text: The carbon atom in an alkane has four sp3 hybridised orbitals and forms four single bonds equidistant from each other (Figure 11.4), so alkane molecules have a tetrahedral shape around each carbon. Carbon atoms in alkanes form sigma bonds with the surrounding carbon and hydrogen atoms, so each carbon is surrounded by four pairs of bonding electrons that repel each other equally, giving bond angles of 109.5 degrees and a C-C bond length of 1.54 angstrom. The shapes of organic molecules are generally represented by ball-and-stick formulas; Table 11.4 shows methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8 and butane C4H10.

Cycloalkanes are cyclic, meaning the carbon atoms of the molecule are arranged in a ring, and saturated, meaning all the ring carbons are singly bonded to other atoms. Table 11.5 shows cyclopropane C3H6, cyclobutane C4H8 and cyclopentane C5H10 (printed C4H10).

blocks.caption: Shapes
rows: two tetrahedral carbons joined by a C-C bond

blocks.prompt: Explain why alkanes have a tetrahedral shape, and draw the shapes of cyclopropane and cyclopentane (Quick Check 11.2b, c).
blocks.explanation: Each alkane carbon is sp3 hybridised with four bonding pairs and no lone pairs; the four pairs repel equally and settle as far apart as possible, at 109.5 degrees, which is the tetrahedral arrangement. Cyclopropane is a triangle of three CH2 groups and cyclopentane a pentagon of five CH2 groups, each corner a carbon.

items: Alkane carbon: sp3, four sigma bonds, tetrahedral, 109.5 degrees, C-C 1.54 angstrom; cycloalkanes are saturated rings (cyclopropane C3H6, cyclobutane C4H8, cyclopentane C5H10).
